When we talk about sound, what’s the first physical quantity that comes to mind? Most people would say sound pressure (p), or sound pressure level. Measuring sound pressure is familiar territory, too: a calibrated microphone does the job. But the wave equation clearly contains another quantity, particle velocity (v, or u), so why do we hear so little about it?

1. What on earth is particle velocity?

A little theory

Let’s go back to before the wave equation, to how sound propagates in a fluid. Sound waves are longitudinal: they travel through the medium as particles move back and forth. Note that these particles are not real physical objects; they are not the molecules of the air. As Professor Kuttruff puts it:

When speaking of particles it is not the molecules of any gas or liquid we have in mind which perform rapid, irregular thermal motions even in absence of sound, instead, we think of particles imagined as small volumes, each of them containing so many molecules that the effects of thermal agitation can be expected to be averaged out [1].

And Professor Jacobsen:

The concept of fluid particles refers to a macroscopic average, not to individual molecules; therefore the particle velocity can be much less than the velocity of the molecules associated with Brownian motion [2].

Both are saying, in essence, that a particle is an average over many of the fluid’s molecules.

Why particle velocity matters

Now that we’ve met particle velocity and the wave equation, a new question may pop up: I can measure sound perfectly well with pressure, and a microphone picks up sound the same way the ear does, so why bother with velocity? There are two reasons.

  1. Acoustic troubleshooting. Close to a source, both the sound pressure and the particle velocity of the propagating wave increase as the distance shrinks. On top of that, because of evanescent waves, v > p in the near field (the derivation is further down).

Meanwhile, on a rigid surface that isn’t radiating sound itself, background noise makes v drop and p rise right at the surface, because velocity is a vector and pressure is a scalar. So background noise no longer gets in the way when particle velocity is used to identify sources.

Together, these two properties make particle velocity a powerful tool for detecting sources in the near field.

2. The key to “energy acoustics.” Everyone knows that sound pressure is the most common quantity in acoustics. But pressure reveals only part of a source’s character, because pressure measurements are strongly affected by the environment. To really understand a source, we need to know what the sound is like at the source itself. That is why, in energy terms, sound power and sound intensity describe a source more precisely. Sound intensity is the product of sound pressure and particle velocity, and sound power can in turn be obtained from the intensity and the surface area or volume. So intensity is the key, and particle velocity is the key to intensity.

2. The particle velocity sensor: the Microflown

Unfortunately, useful as particle velocity is, for a long time nobody could measure it accurately. Then, in 1994, Hans-Elias de Bree at the University of Twente in the Netherlands invented the Microflown, a sensor that measures particle velocity in air, and particle velocity could be captured directly for the first time. Four years later, he and Alex Koers founded Microflown Technologies, named after the sensor.

A one-dimensional probe, with a MEMS microphone and a Microflown particle velocity sensor built in

The three-dimensional USP (Ultimate Sound Probe). It also contains a MEMS microphone, plus three Microflown sensors arranged orthogonally, so it can measure particle velocity in 3D and hence sound intensity in 3D.

[https://www.microflown.com/products/standard-probes/usp-regular/]

How the Microflown works

Two ultra-thin platinum resistance wires are heated to a set temperature. When a sound wave passes, heat is exchanged and both wires cool down. But because the air particles have already been warmed by the first wire, the second wire cools less than the first, and this creates a difference in resistance. Across the audible frequency range, that resistance difference is proportional to the particle velocity [3,4].

What makes the Microflown special

These unusual traits give the Microflown clear advantages over conventional microphone-based techniques:

  • It can be used in the field amid loud background noise and still capture signals with a high signal-to-noise ratio

  • Its strong directivity is frequency-independent: it keeps its figure-of-eight pattern down to 20 Hz

Applications

Put a Microflown and a microphone in the same probe, and you can measure sound pressure, particle velocity and sound intensity to your heart’s content!

With all this, Mom never has to worry about my source localization again! Just grab the probe, sweep it around, and you’re done.

Locating leaks in oil and gas pipelines at a plant, for example,

or, in NVH, locating sound sources inside a car.

Motorcycles are no exception.

The source maps are results from Microflown’s Scan&Paint 2D scanning system [https://www.microflown.com/case-studies/noise-reduction-on-a-high-performance-two-wheeler/]

Not satisfied with 2D? Let’s go 3D. The sound field that a car audio system produces inside the cabin can be visualized in three dimensions, down to 20 Hz. So besides localizing sources, the method can also visualize the sound field itself.

All the 3D vector plots are results from Microflown’s Scan&Paint 3D scanning system

Visualizations of three fields. Particle velocity and intensity are vector fields, so you can see which way the sound is traveling

Aircraft are no problem either.

3D scan vector plot of an Airbus cabin

How exactly are these images produced, and what does the measurement involve? Tune in next time, or the time after, for the scan-based imaging technique, Scan & Paint.

Afterword

Another ten hours or so. Luckily this one isn’t a history, so I didn’t have to read quite so much. Then again, once you dive into the equations, it takes a while to surface… The good news is that I’ve finally started the first article in a popular-science series; the histories will continue, on an irregular schedule. This line of articles will go on to sound intensity, including active and reactive intensity, which I find fascinating, and to detailed industrial case studies using particle velocity and intensity. I’ve also come up with a few fun bits of acoustics trivia that I’ll write up when I have time.
